stories.headline: Wolf Creek Pass could reopen to limited traffic this weekend after catastrophic flooding
stories.summary:
Limited traffic may be allowed over Wolf Creek Pass as early as this weekend, the Colorado Department of Transportation said Tuesday, as crews work around the clock on repairs to U.S. 160 after catastrophic flooding in southwestern Colorado. Four teams have been clearing debris since Monday, including 6 to 8 feet of rocks and mud across the west side of the pass. Other crews are stabilizing sections of road that crumbled, leaving guardrails "hanging in thin air," said Julie Constan, CDOT's Region 5 director.

The pass normally carries 2,700 to 3,400 vehicles per day and connects South Fork and Pagosa Springs. When it is closed, travelers must detour through New Mexico. "It's not going to be your normal trip across Wolf Creek Pass, but at least we'll be able to get people through and across," Constan said.

After the first of two historic back-to-back storms, CDOT requested $65 million in federal aid. Executive Director Shoshana Lew said the figure is likely to rise to about $100 million, with a refined estimate expected in the coming days.

Crews must rebuild the permanent U.S. 160 bridge west of Pagosa Springs and install a temporary span, which officials expect to open with one lane in each direction by mid-January. The permanent bridge is expected to be finished by the end of 2027. Crews are also working to allow limited traffic on Colorado 151 by Thanksgiving.

stories.headline: Phil Weiser selects top Senate Republican, Denver official for first cabinet roles
stories.summary:
One week after winning the governor's race in a landslide, Gov.-elect Phil Weiser on Tuesday nominated Cleave Simpson, the Republican minority leader in the state Senate, to be Colorado's next agriculture commissioner. The pick brings a prominent, moderate conservative into the incoming Democratic administration.

Weiser also chose Dominick Moreno, a former state senator and currently deputy chief operating officer for Denver Mayor Mike Johnston, as budget director. Jeni Arndt, a former lawmaker and Fort Collins mayor, will serve as director of rural advancement, and deputy attorney general Scott Steinbrecher will become water adviser. The rural and water posts are new cabinet-level positions that fulfill campaign pledges.

Many of the appointments, including Simpson's, must be confirmed by the state Senate. If Simpson is confirmed next year, a vacancy committee will appoint his replacement in the legislature, and Senate Republicans are scheduled to elect new caucus leadership Saturday.

Separately, newly elected Treasurer Jeff Bridges named Gov. Jared Polis's budget director, Mark Ferrandino, as his deputy treasurer. Weiser has said more cabinet picks will come in the coming months and has also pledged a chief housing officer.

stories.headline: Broncos agree to trade with Chargers for linebacker Daiyan Henley
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos have agreed to terms on a trade with the Los Angeles Chargers to acquire linebacker Daiyan Henley, pending a physical, according to the team's website. The move was reported by lead writer Aric DiLalla.

The deal comes a day after Denver beat the Carolina Panthers 26-21 in Week 9. The team has also dealt with injuries in its defensive backfield in recent weeks.

The trade becomes official once Henley passes his physical. Further details of the compensation were not included in the team's initial report.

stories.headline: Denver police release body-camera video of Oct. 23 shooting in north Denver
stories.summary:
Denver police released new body-camera video showing the moments officers came under gunfire while responding to a domestic violence call in north Denver on Oct. 23. The department said the outcome was deadly and one that nobody wanted.

All seven officers involved had their body cameras activated and have been placed on modified duty. Chief Thomas said the department did not want the incident to end this way.

Four agencies are involved in the investigation. The Denver District Attorney's Office will determine whether the officers' use of force was legally justified.

stories.headline: Police seek suspect in overnight stabbing near Colfax and Washington
stories.summary:
Denver police are searching for a suspect after a man was stabbed overnight near Colfax Avenue and Washington Street. The Denver Police Department announced the investigation on social media.

The victim's condition and a suspect description were not detailed in the initial report. Police have not said what led to the stabbing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Denver police or Crime Stoppers.

stories.headline: Westminster police seek help identifying apartment burglary suspect
stories.summary:
Westminster police are asking the public for help identifying a man linked to a burglary at an apartment in the city. According to the report, a woman confronted the suspect inside her apartment.

Police have released information intended to help identify the man. Further details about what was taken or the timing of the incident were not included in the initial report.

Anyone who recognizes the suspect is asked to contact Westminster police.

stories.headline: Albuquerque cardiac health firm Karoo Health relocates to Denver
stories.summary:
Karoo Health, a venture-backed cardiac health startup founded in Albuquerque in 2021, is moving its headquarters to Denver, citing difficulty attracting talent in New Mexico. The company has signed a three-year lease for offices at 1925 Blake St. in downtown Denver.

CEO Ian Koons said Denver offers a "talent density far superior" to Albuquerque. The firm has about 80 corporate employees spread across the country, and he hopes to bring about 80% of them to the Denver office. Koons said Karoo did not seek relocation incentives from Colorado officials.

Karoo partners with cardiology practices to connect patients to services such as nutritionists and pharmacists, and shares savings with insurers and providers when costs fall. It has raised nearly $35 million, including a $16.2 million Series A round this summer, and serves nearly 20,000 patients through 700 cardiology providers in 12 states.

stories.headline: Denver middle-market firms weigh hiring, housing and commute costs of growth
stories.summary:
A Denver Business Journal report examines how middle-market companies in the Denver area are navigating the costs of growth, including hiring and housing. Downtown office attendance remains down 50% from 2019, adding to the challenge of commercial vacancy.

Executives are rethinking facility locations, shift structures and even customer service models based on commute reliability. With housing costs pushing workers farther from job sites, some companies are relocating to reduce commute friction, while others are keeping flexible in-office schedule requirements.

The report is by Brett Forrest, a Denver Business Journal reporter.

stories.headline: Denver council candidate proposes housing on RTD station parking lots to fund frequent trains
stories.summary:
Denver City Council District 10 candidate June Churchill has proposed turning largely empty transit parking lots into housing, using the recurring revenue to support trains arriving every 15 minutes. She outlined the idea in a Transit Tangents video.

Under the proposed agreement, RTD would provide a contractual guarantee of frequent service, while Denver would offer infrastructure support and density bonuses for development. Churchill said RTD station lots have vacancy rates around 80%, and that lease income would give the agency steadier revenue than the sales tax that provides most of its budget.

Churchill said Denver needs roughly 70,000 more homes within 25 years and pointed to potential sites including the Summit FC stadium site, Burnham Yards and River Mile. RTD is conducting a comprehensive operational analysis with Jarrett Walker Associates to rethink bus service, according to Greater Denver Transit co-founder James Flattum.

stories.headline: Opinion: Colorado's two strong parties are both inside the Democratic Party
stories.summary:
A Colorado Newsline analysis argues that Colorado's policy debates are now being fought between factions within the Democratic Party. Gov.-elect Phil Weiser won 61% of the vote to Republican Victor Marx's 33% and called on the state GOP to become a more serious party.

The piece describes a progressive movement pushing state policy left and a moderate bloc responsive to business concerns about taxes and regulation. Disputes over oil and gas, housing affordability, criminal justice and labor law continue, now largely within the majority party.

Democrats return to the statehouse in January with unprecedented supermajorities in both chambers. The analysis cites LegiScan roll-call data to show the intra-party divide.

stories.headline: Warm, dry weather to continue along Front Range, with possible pattern change next week
stories.summary:
The Denver metro area will stay warm and dry this week, with temperatures running 10 to 15 degrees above average. Tuesday highs were expected in the upper 60s to near 70, with increasing afternoon clouds and no precipitation statewide.

A weak cold front will bring gusty winds to the northeastern plains Tuesday afternoon and evening, which could elevate fire danger. Highs Wednesday will dip slightly but remain in the low to mid 60s, above the normal 55 degrees. Thursday and Friday could reach the upper 60s to low 70s.

Light rain and snow showers are possible in the mountains Saturday, while lower elevations stay mostly dry. Late next week, a pattern change could bring heavier mountain snow and perhaps the first flakes of the season in Denver.

weather.notable: About 12 degrees above the average high for this time of year!

topStory.headline: House Votes 211-204 to Send Hegseth Impeachment Articles to Committee, Stalling Effort for Now
topStory.summary:
The Republican-led House of Representatives on Tuesday voted 211-204 to refer articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively halting the effort for the time being. The resolution, introduced Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., contained eight articles alleging violations of federal law and the Constitution in connection with the war in Iran and other military operations in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean. Massie was the only Republican to vote with Democrats to keep the resolution alive.

Massie filed the measure as a privileged resolution, which required House leaders to schedule a vote within two legislative days. He argued that Hegseth "has violated the norms of war, and it's to the disadvantage and the dishonor of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflicts." Massie, an outspoken critic of both Hegseth and President Donald Trump, lost his GOP primary earlier this year after opposition from both men, and is leaving Congress. Even some Republican critics of Hegseth said they did not believe his actions rose to the level of "high crimes and misdemeanors."

Hegseth held a Pentagon news conference Tuesday morning, calling the effort a "political spectacle," "a farce" and "a stunt." He maintained that all of the military actions cited were lawful and said the impeachment was an affront to service members carrying them out. He likened the vote to the two Democratic-led impeachments of Trump in his first term, saying, "If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I'll take that company every day of the week." Trump said Hegseth "gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" and, after the vote, called the outcome an "EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot." Vice President JD Vance has called the suggestion that Hegseth committed impeachable offenses "absurd."

The committee referral does not entirely rule out a future impeachment vote, but it sends the matter to the Judiciary Committee with no clear timeline. Democrats are set to take control of the House in January, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is on track to become speaker, has said Democrats will "run Pete Hegseth out of town." Any renewed effort would still face a high bar, as removal from office would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate. Hegseth has also clashed with a handful of Republicans in both chambers, and Vance has blamed the Iran war for Republican losses in the midterm elections.
